paras: The killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas, took place on a plantation in Wharton County in the third week of March 1888, a few weeks after a massacre of Black residents at the same settlement. The victims were not named and no one was reported arrested. Papers treated the killings as fresh proof of a 'reign of terror' against the county's Black population that state rangers had failed to stop.

Spanish Camp had recently been the scene of a massacre in which six Black people were shot and their house burned over them. After that killing, Governor L. S. Ross sent a company of state rangers into Wharton County to help the local authorities keep the peace. According to a Houston correspondent, the rangers' presence had not calmed the area, and many people were leaving after receiving an "invitation to quit the country."

A courier who reached Richmond, Texas, from Wharton reported that two Black men had been murdered on Tuesday night on Battel's plantation, near the scene of the earlier massacre. A later Richmond dispatch of March 26 referred instead to the "Thursday night murders" on "the Battled place." No report described how the men were killed or who killed them, and a Houston special of March 23 said that no particulars had arrived.

Threats against others continued at the same time. James Wygall of Clarke plantation, near Spanish Camp, arrived at Richmond carrying a rifle and said he had left because of a letter warning him to leave the county. The March 26 dispatch named Henry Wyatt, described as a well-to-do white farmer, as one of the threatened white "sympathizers" who had fled to Richmond, adding that people in his position had no faith that the rangers could prevent their assassination.

Governor Ross was reported as saying he would send the whole military force of the state if necessary to suppress "the lawless element." Rangers were ordered to report to the sheriff at Wharton to keep the peace during the coming session of the district court, when, the dispatch said, the assassins were expected to be denounced before the grand jury. No report of an indictment or trial for the two killings appears in the coverage, and by late May the ranger detachment in Wharton County had been ordered to Hempstead.

At the Republican state convention in April, Colonel DeGress moved to endorse Ross's action in the "recent race troubles in Wharton and other counties," praising a governor who had "the courage to protect the lives of the humble citizens of the colored race."

The first reports appeared on March 24 from two separate sources: a Houston special to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and a Richmond courier dispatch carried by wire through Chicago. The Gazette headed its story "MORE BLOOD" and "Another Slaughter of Colored People," yet closed by saying that the facts, though from a reliable source, were discredited in Houston. The San Antonio Daily Light took a sharper line, writing that the men were killed "in cold blood" and calling for the "butchers of law-abiding citizens" to be punished even with the aid of the national government.

Outside Texas the Richmond dispatch ran under heads such as "Texan Lawlessness" in the Memphis Appeal and "Negroes Murdered in Texas" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, and in the Indianapolis Journal on March 25. Dakota weeklies printed the fuller March 26 version in early April, including its belief that a secret society of white planters had been organized "for the purpose of expelling and killing obnoxious negroes and their white sympathizers." A one-line roundup item, reprinted as late as April 11 in South Carolina, stated flatly that "armed whites have again murdered two negroes."

The two Richmond dispatches disagree on the night of the killings, Tuesday in the earlier and Thursday in the later. Both also describe a threatened white farmer from near Spanish Camp arriving at Richmond, named James Wygall in one and Henry Wyatt in the other, without saying whether these were the same man.

reader.title: Killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas (March 1888)
bases: Two Black men were killed by unnamed attackers amid threatening letters and 'invitations' to leave the county, which one dispatch believed were the work of a secret society of white planters organized to expel and kill (A5, A6, A17).

A Houston special (A5) and a separate Richmond, Tex. courier dispatch (A6, A17) both report two more Black men killed near Spanish Camp, though the Houston correspondent added that the report was discredited in Houston (A5).

accounts.label: Houston special to the Fort Worth Gazette
accounts.gist: News of a double killing at Spanish Camp reached Houston with no particulars; rangers' presence had not calmed the area and people were leaving after invitations to quit, but the report was discredited in Houston.

accounts.label: Richmond, Tex. courier dispatch (Mar. 24-25)
accounts.gist: A courier from Wharton said two negroes were murdered Tuesday night on Battel's plantation near Spanish Camp; a white planter, James Wygall, had fled after a threatening letter.

accounts.label: Richmond, Tex. dispatch (Mar. 26)
accounts.gist: The 'Thursday night murders' on the Battel place were part of a 'reign of terror' among the county's Black population, believed to be the work of a secret society of white planters; Henry Wyatt had fled, and rangers were to guard the coming district court and grand jury.

accounts.label: Syndicated news brief
accounts.gist: Armed whites had again murdered two negroes at Spanish Camp, and the governor sent rangers.

framing.detail: The San Antonio Daily Light wrote of two negroes killed 'in cold blood', called the killers 'butchers of law-abiding citizens', and urged the state or the federal government to punish them.
The Fort Worth Gazette headed its Houston special 'MORE BLOOD' and 'Another Slaughter of Colored People' but added that the report was discredited in Houston.
Papers outside Texas ran the Richmond courier dispatch under heads such as 'Two Negroes Killed', 'Texan Lawlessness' and 'Negroes Murdered in Texas', or a one-line brief in news roundups.
The Mar. 26 Richmond dispatch described a 'reign of terror' and compared conditions with Kemper County, Mississippi, twelve years earlier.

conflicts.note: The earlier dispatch (Mar. 24) says Tuesday; the Mar. 26 version says Thursday. Both fall before the Houston report of Mar. 23 only if 'Thursday' is Mar. 22; neither is clearly better.

versions.value: From a reliable source but 'discredited in this city' (Houston)

conflicts.note: Later Richmond dispatches repeated the killings without doubt; no report contradicting the facts was found.

conflicts.note: Both dispatches came from Richmond, Tex., and both describe a white farmer from near Spanish Camp arriving after threats; they may describe the same man under different spellings, but the papers do not say so.

record_check.dossier: About Mar. 20, 1888 (Tuesday night, per the Mar. 24 dispatch) or Mar. 22 (Thursday night, per the Mar. 26 version); first reported Mar. 23-24.
Killing of two Black men by unnamed attackers amid a threat-and-expulsion campaign; closer to whitecapping (or a lynching by an unidentified band) than a mob assault.
Unknown; 'armed whites' in one brief; a secret society of white planters only 'believed' responsible.
Every report of this episode gives two killed; six (or more) belongs to the earlier February massacre at Spanish Camp.
